title: Hepatic Lipidosis
desc: Sharon Center's feline hepatic lipidosis protocol — feeding tube first, l-carnitine, taurine, B vitamins, zinc, vitamin E, SAMe or NAC, and the fluid and refeeding cautions.

meds.name: L-carnitine
meds.desc: the single biggest survival gain in this protocol
meds.note: Dr Center reports survival rising from 62.5% to 85.3% with the addition of l-carnitine to the protocol.

meds.name: Thiamine
meds.desc: only if there is ventroflexion of the neck
meds.doseText: 100 to 200 mg per day for 3 days
meds.note: Give if the cat shows ventroflexion of the neck. Ventroflexion in a cat is also a classic sign of hypokalaemia — check potassium as well.

meds.name: SAMe
meds.note: Either SAMe or N-acetylcysteine — SAMe once the cat is being fed enterally, NAC while it is not.

meds.name: N-acetylcysteine
meds.desc: IV glutathione source, before enteral feeding is established
freqs: IV twice daily until enteral feeding is established
meds.note: LOADING DOSE 140 mg/kg IV first, then 70 mg/kg IV BID (the figure calculated above is the maintenance dose, not the load) until enteral feeding is established.

meds.grp: If the primary process is inflammatory
meds.name: Fish oil
meds.note: Supplies omega-3 PUFAs, which are anti-inflammatory if the primary process is an inflammatory one.

notes.Source: Treatment of hepatic lipidosis after Sharon Center.
notes.Protein: Do NOT feed a diet low in protein. Protein restriction is the classic mistake in these cats.
notes.Underlying disease: Treat the underlying disease — hepatic lipidosis is almost always secondary to something else.
notes.Before a feeding tube: Check for bleeding tendencies (low vitamin K) BEFORE placing an esophagostomy or PEG tube.
notes.Electrolytes: Supplement potassium and phosphorus as needed, and watch for hypophosphataemia developing after refeeding begins.
notes.Carnitine: Dr Center has seen survival rise from 62.5% to 85.3% with l-carnitine added to the protocol.

dischargeBlocks.title: What has happened
dischargeBlocks.text:
When a cat stops eating, the body moves fat into the liver faster than the liver can process it. The liver becomes clogged with fat and stops working properly, and the cat feels too ill to eat — which makes it worse.

Breaking that cycle means getting food into {name} reliably, every day, whether or not there is any appetite. That is the whole treatment.

dischargeBlocks.title: The feeding tube
dischargeBlocks.text:
The feeding tube is not a sign that things have gone badly — it is the treatment, and it is what turns this condition around.

- Feed the amounts we have written down, at the times we have written down, even if {name} seems to be eating a little alone.
- Warm the food to about body temperature and give it slowly.
- Flush the tube with water before and after every feed.
- Keep the bandage clean and dry, and look at the skin around the tube each day.

Do not remove the tube yourself, and do not stop using it once {name} starts to nibble — we will tell you when it can come out.

dischargeBlocks.title: Food
dischargeBlocks.text: {name} needs a high-protein diet. Please do not switch to a low-protein or "liver" diet, and do not give a home-cooked diet unless we have designed it — protein restriction makes this condition worse, not better.

dischargeBlocks.title: Call us if
dischargeBlocks.text:
- {name} vomits repeatedly, or vomits after tube feeds
- The tube becomes blocked, moves, or comes out
- The skin around the tube is red, swollen, smelly or discharging
- {name} becomes weak, floppy, or cannot hold the head up normally
- There is any yellow colour to the gums, eyes or skin

A cat that cannot hold its head up needs to be seen the same day.

dischargeBlocks.title: Follow up
dischargeBlocks.text: We need to recheck {name} and repeat bloodwork on the schedule we discussed. Recovery takes weeks and the tube usually stays in for most of that — please keep every appointment even when {name} looks better.
